title: Urological Guidelines for Kidney Stones: Overview and Comprehensive Update
condition_or_topic: Kidney stone disease (KSD) and urolithiasis management guidelines
clinical_background: Urolithiasis is common worldwide, although its occurrence varies with factors such as sex, climate and diet. Stone prevalence has risen annually among people older than 30. Treatment of KSD was estimated to cost USD 5.3 billion globally in 2014, making it the second most costly urological condition. The American Urological Association (AUA) and European Association of Urology (EAU) publish widely used guidance on diagnosis, treatment and follow-up. Their approaches to grading evidence and recommendations differ. Although guidelines provide an evidence-based framework, the article notes that they cannot guarantee the best outcome for an individual patient.
objectives: Provide guidance on KSD management by reviewing and comparing the AUA and EAU recommendations for medical and surgical care.
Evaluate the evidence and recommendation grades presented in the AUA and EAU urolithiasis guidelines.
study_design: Narrative review comparing the evidence and recommendation grades in the AUA and EAU guidelines for the medical and surgical management of urolithiasis.
interpretation: The AUA and EAU guidelines largely agree on the principles of kidney stone management, although recommendations differ in some situations involving stone size and treatment selection. The authors regard the guidelines as evidence-based frameworks for care, not as guarantees of the best outcome for an individual patient.
clinical_implications: Differences in stone location, size, composition, patient circumstances and available surgical expertise can affect which management option is appropriate.
For patients requiring stone removal, URS generally offers a higher stone-free rate than SWL, whereas SWL has fewer complications and lower morbidity.
For large renal stones, PCNL offers a higher stone-free rate and reduces the need for secondary procedures, but its greater morbidity matters when discussing treatment choices.
In an infected obstructed urinary system, sepsis makes prompt drainage and antimicrobial treatment particularly important.
practice_implications: Use the guidelines to inform an individualised treatment plan that takes account of patient preferences, surgical expertise and other patient-specific factors; do not allow the guidelines to supersede clinical judgment.

Assess the patient's history and examination at presentation, provide effective analgesia without waiting for imaging, and expedite investigation when the diagnosis is unclear, pyrexia is present or the patient has a solitary kidney, as recommended by the EAU.

Select imaging according to symptoms and clinical context: the EAU recommends US initially for asymptomatic patients and NCCT for symptomatic patients; both guidelines support urine culture and microscopy before intervention.

Consider observation with active surveillance for suitable uncomplicated stones. For non-obstructing renal stones managed conservatively, the EAU recommends a first review at 6 months and annual reviews thereafter.

Follow the applicable guideline and clinical scenario when considering α-blockers as MET for distal ureteral stones; the article gives differing size thresholds in its accounts of the EAU recommendations. The AUA suggests a 4–6 weeks trial before formulating a definitive treatment plan if MET has not succeeded.

Offer urgent decompression by PCN or ureteric stenting for sepsis associated with obstruction, start antibiotics without delay and defer definitive stone treatment until sepsis has resolved, in accordance with both guidelines.

For renal stones >20 mm, both guidelines recommend PCNL as first-line treatment. For lower-pole stones of 10–20 mm, account for the differing AUA and EAU positions on first-line SWL and discuss the greater stone-free rate and morbidity associated with PCNL.

Adapt investigation and treatment for children and pregnant patients as described by the respective guidelines, including radiation-conscious imaging in children and a multidisciplinary approach during pregnancy.
Arrange stone analysis and risk-based metabolic evaluation to guide recurrence prevention. Both guidelines emphasise fluid intake sufficient to produce a 24-h urinary volume of at least >2.5 L.

After endourological treatment or SWL, consider follow-up imaging and management of residual fragments in light of clinical judgment and patient preferences; the EAU cautions that imaging within 4 weeks may prompt overtreatment because stone dust can produce false-positive findings.
limitations: Guidelines cannot ensure the best outcome for every patient, particularly because keeping them current has limitations.

The natural history and progression risk of small, non-obstructing renal stones are insufficiently defined, and both guidelines identify a lack of high-quality evidence for observation in this setting.
High-quality evidence is sparse on when to image after a procedure and when to treat residual fragments.
The article notes insufficient evidence for some paediatric decisions, including observation of stones and imaging for suspected bladder stones.
Comparative clinical evidence remains insufficient to establish how TFL performs relative to Ho:YAG in URS.
strengths: The guidelines cover a broad range of diagnostic, medical and surgical decisions using evidence-based approaches.
Despite some differences, the AUA and EAU recommendations agree on most general management principles.
open_questions: How accurately should stone size determine treatment selection?
Which practices in endourology are best supported by further evaluation of the evidence?
What is the natural history and progression risk of small, non-obstructing renal stones?
How do TFL and Ho:YAG compare in further clinical studies?
future_directions: Update guidelines regularly as new evidence becomes available, including evidence on new lasers, day-case surgery, smaller scopes, artificial intelligence and suction devices.
Include costs and patient-reported outcomes in future studies.
Use more consistent definitions and reporting of measurable, comparable outcomes to improve comparisons between studies, patient counselling and decision-making.

main_conclusion: The authors find that the AUA and EAU guidelines agree on most principles of stone management, although some recommendations differ by stone size and clinical setting. They call for regular updates and for treatment plans that account for patient preferences, surgical expertise and individual circumstances.
narrative_summary:
This review compares AUA and EAU guidance on the assessment, medical treatment, procedures and prevention of urinary stones, including care in children, pregnancy and renal transplant recipients. The authors assess the evidence and recommendation grades presented in the guidelines rather than reporting outcomes from a new patient cohort. Both organisations address imaging, treatment selection and metabolic evaluation, and their principal management recommendations largely align, with differences in some stone-size thresholds and preferred interventions.

The review describes NCCT as central to evaluating symptomatic stones and planning selected procedures, while US has an initial role in asymptomatic patients, children and pregnancy. For infected obstruction with sepsis, both guidelines recommend urgent drainage, prompt antibiotics and postponement of definitive stone treatment until sepsis resolves. URS generally provides a higher stone-free rate than SWL, whereas SWL has fewer complications; PCNL is first-line for renal stones >20 mm. Recommendations for lower-pole stones of 10–20 mm differ, particularly over when SWL is appropriate. Prevention guidance includes stone analysis, risk-based metabolic assessment and fluid intake sufficient for 24-h urinary volume of at least >2.5 L. The authors emphasise that guidelines are a framework, not a substitute for individualised decisions, and advocate regular updates and more consistent reporting of patient-reported outcomes and comparable endpoints.

main_findings.description: The AUA and EAU guidelines broadly agree on the management of urolithiasis, although some recommendations differ, particularly those based on stone size.
main_findings.context: This article compares guidelines; it does not report a primary endpoint or original treatment-effect estimates.

main_findings.description: For asymptomatic patients, the EAU recommends US as initial imaging. For symptomatic patients, it recommends NCCT, which provides stone and anatomical information for treatment selection and is more precise than US or IVU.
main_findings.context: EAU: strong recommendation for NCCT in symptomatic patients. The EAU recommends contrast-enhanced imaging when collecting-system anatomy must be assessed before stone removal.

main_findings.description: The AUA recommends NCCT before PCNL and considers it when choosing between SWL and URS; it discourages using US alone for that treatment choice. Functional imaging can help guide treatment if substantial renal injury is suspected.
main_findings.context: AUA: strong recommendation for NCCT before PCNL; conditional recommendation for NCCT when selecting SWL or URS and for functional imaging.

main_findings.description: For suspected bladder stones in symptomatic patients, the EAU recommends US first, followed by consideration of NCCT or cystoscopy if symptoms persist and US is inconclusive. X-ray KUB has low accuracy for detecting these stones.
main_findings.context: EAU: strong recommendation for the imaging sequence; weak recommendation for use of X-ray KUB in treatment planning and follow-up. The AUA gives no bladder-stone diagnostic guidance.

main_findings.description: The EAU recommends laboratory assessment when intervention is planned, and both the AUA and EAU strongly recommend urine culture and microscopy before intervention.
main_findings.context: The EAU specifies serum creatinine, uric acid, ionised calcium, sodium, potassium, blood cell counts, C-reactive protein and coagulation tests.

main_findings.description: The review reports evidence from cited meta-analyses of a class effect of α-blockers as off-label MET. Guideline thresholds for distal ureteral stones differ, and the article gives inconsistent EAU thresholds in different sections.
main_findings.value: EAU: >5 mm in section 3.1; <5 mm in section 4.3.1; AUA: ≤10 mm
main_findings.context: Both sections label the respective α-blocker recommendations as strong; the conflicting EAU thresholds are retained as reported.

main_findings.description: The AUA suggests a trial of MET before formulating a definitive treatment plan if treatment has not succeeded; the EAU specifies no interval between MET and definitive treatment.
main_findings.context: Duration applies to the AUA approach; AUA: moderate recommendation.

main_findings.description: Urinary alkalinisation with alkaline citrate or sodium bicarbonate can dissolve uric acid stones, but the article reports that RCTs of oral chemolitholysis are unavailable. The AUA considers stone dissolution with potassium citrate in uric acid and cystine stones inconsistent.
main_findings.context: AUA: expert opinion concerning potassium citrate. The EAU strongly recommends monitoring urinary pH and adjusting treatment during and after chemolysis.

main_findings.description: Compared with URS and PCNL, SWL has a lower SFR but fewer overall complications. Compared specifically with SWL, URS has a higher SFR and is less likely to require another procedure.
main_findings.context: Comparative findings are presented from cited literature; the article supplies no numerical effect estimates.

main_findings.description: Routine stenting before SWL is discouraged by the AUA. The EAU reports no SFR improvement with routine stenting, although it may reduce steinstrasse. Both guidelines discuss α-blockers after SWL to facilitate fragment passage.
main_findings.context: AUA: strong recommendation against routine stenting and moderate recommendation for off-label α-blockers after SWL.

main_findings.description: Neither guideline recommends routine stenting before URS. For patients without increased postprocedural complication risk, both recommend avoiding a stent after URS because of morbidity and cost; if a stent is placed, they recommend α-blockers for discomfort.
main_findings.context: AUA: strong recommendation against routine pre-stenting. Postprocedural stent avoidance: EAU/AUA: strong recommendation. α-blockers for stent discomfort: EAU: strong recommendation; AUA: moderate recommendation.

main_findings.description: The EAU recommends Ho:YAG for URS across stone types. It describes TFL results as apparently equivalent but states that further comparative clinical studies are needed.
main_findings.context: EAU: strong recommendation for Ho:YAG.

main_findings.description: PCNL is preferred for most large renal stones because its SFR is higher and its effectiveness is less dependent on stone burden or composition. The EAU describes mini-PNL as having similar SFR, shorter hospital stay and less blood loss than standard PCNL.
main_findings.context: The article gives no numerical SFR, length-of-stay or blood-loss estimates.

main_findings.description: After uncomplicated PCNL, the guidelines advise considering tubeless or totally tubeless approaches, which are linked to shorter hospital stays and improved postoperative pain control.
main_findings.context: EAU: strong recommendation; AUA: conditional recommendation.

main_findings.description: The EAU recommends obtaining a renal-pelvic urine culture or stone culture during PCNL because sepsis may occur despite a sterile preoperative urine culture; a pelvic culture may better anticipate sepsis and guide antibiotic selection.
main_findings.context: EAU: strong recommendation.

main_findings.description: Open or laparoscopic stone removal is reserved for situations in which SWL, URS and PCNL are unlikely to succeed. The AUA identifies stones accompanied by anatomical defects requiring reconstruction as a possible setting.
main_findings.context: EAU/AUA: strong recommendation for restricting these approaches.

main_findings.description: For acute renal colic, paracetamol and NSAIDs provide better pain relief than opioids and are recommended first after contraindications have been excluded. Persistent pain despite analgesia warrants decompression and endoscopic stone removal.
main_findings.context: EAU: strong recommendation.

main_findings.description: For sepsis associated with an infected obstructed urinary system, both guidelines recommend urgent decompression by PCN or ureteric stenting, without evidence that either method is superior; definitive stone treatment is delayed until sepsis resolves.
main_findings.context: EAU/AUA: strong recommendation. Antibiotics should begin without delay and may be revised when sensitivities become available.

main_findings.description: Observation with reassessment is an option for uncomplicated ureteral stones. The EAU gives no numerical stone-size cutoff and notes that spontaneous passage becomes less likely as stone size increases, whereas the AUA specifies a cutoff.
main_findings.context: EAU/AUA: strong recommendation.

main_findings.description: Active removal of ureteral stones is indicated when spontaneous passage is unlikely, obstruction is present, pain persists despite adequate analgesia, or renal function is reduced because of renal failure, a solitary kidney or bilateral obstruction.
main_findings.context: The article presents SWL and URS as active treatment options.

main_findings.description: For proximal or distal ureteral stones above the EAU size threshold, the EAU favours URS first; below that threshold, it allows either URS or SWL. The AUA favours URS for mid- and distal-ureteral stones requiring intervention but does not extend that preference to larger proximal-ureteral stones, for which its panel did not find superior SFR with URS over SWL.
main_findings.value: EAU: >10 mm for first-line URS; <10 mm for URS or SWL; AUA proximal ureter exception: > 10 mm
main_findings.context: The AUA recommendation for URS in the mid- and distal ureter is strong; its stated SFR advantage is particularly relevant for stones <10 mm. The ureteral-stone table has a location-row inconsistency, so the comparison follows the explanatory text.

main_findings.description: Selected asymptomatic, non-obstructing calyceal stones can be observed, but the natural history and progression risk of small non-obstructing stones remain uncertain. Both guidelines advise surveillance when observation is chosen.
main_findings.value: EAU: 6 months for the first follow-up and yearly thereafter
main_findings.context: AUA: conditional recommendation for observation and no specified surveillance interval. Both guidelines note a lack of high-quality evidence for this approach.

main_findings.description: The EAU reports that SWL is unlikely to work for renal stones above the stated density threshold and recommends assessing stone composition before active treatment.
main_findings.context: EAU: strong recommendation.

main_findings.description: For renal-pelvis or upper/middle-calyceal stones above the larger size threshold, both guidelines favour PCNL because of higher SFR and less need for secondary procedures. For smaller stones, recommendations include SWL or URS; the EAU also includes PCNL among the options in the intermediate size range.
main_findings.value: >20 mm: PCNL first line; <20 mm: SWL or URS as first-line options in the AUA text; EAU 10–20 mm: SWL, URS or PCNL; EAU <10 mm: SWL or URS first line, PCNL second line
main_findings.context: AUA/EAU: strong recommendation for PCNL at >20 mm. The AUA strongly recommends SWL or URS for <20 mm in this location.

main_findings.description: For lower-pole calculi in the intermediate size range, the AUA strongly advises against SWL as first-line treatment and advises explaining the higher SFR and greater morbidity of PCNL. The EAU permits first-line SWL when factors are favourable but favours PCNL when unfavourable factors are present.
main_findings.context: The EAU identifies a narrow infundibulum, long skin-to-stone distance, long calyx, shock-wave-resistant stones and a steep infundibular-pelvic angle as unfavourable for SWL.

main_findings.description: For adults with bladder stones, the EAU favours transurethral cystolithotripsy first and percutaneous cystolithotripsy if the transurethral approach is not feasible. Transurethral, endoscopic and percutaneous approaches have similar SFRs and shorter operative, hospital and catheterisation durations than open cystolithotomy; SWL has a lower SFR than open or endoscopic procedures.
main_findings.context: EAU: strong recommendation for transurethral treatment and consideration of a percutaneous alternative; weak recommendation for open cystolithotomy as a first-line option for very large stones.

main_findings.description: After endourology or SWL, the EAU recommends imaging for residual fragments. NCCT detects fragments more sensitively than X-ray, US or IVU, but its radiation exposure and detection of clinically insignificant particles must be weighed against that advantage.
main_findings.context: The EAU cautions that imaging within 4 weeks may yield false positives from dust particles and lead to overtreatment; it leaves timing and treatment decisions to clinical judgment and patient preferences.

main_findings.description: Both guidelines recommend analysing a first-time stone when available and assessing recurrence risk and metabolic factors. The review reports that dietary advice tailored to metabolic findings prevents recurrence more effectively than general dietary advice.
main_findings.context: The dietary comparison is attributed to cited evidence, without a numerical estimate. The EAU strongly recommends first-time stone analysis; the AUA presents it as a clinical principle.

main_findings.description: Metabolic assessment uses urinary collections, preferably two according to the AUA and two consecutive collections according to the EAU. The patient should ideally be stone-free and eating a usual diet before initial testing.
main_findings.value: one or two 24-h urinary samples; at least 20 days stone-free
main_findings.context: The EAU also permits consideration of spot urine when 24-h collection is not possible, while noting its limited usefulness.

main_findings.description: Both guidelines emphasise fluid intake to reduce stone-formation risk and recommend a minimum urinary-volume target.
main_findings.context: EAU: strong recommendation; AUA: standard.

main_findings.description: For recurrent calcium stones without abnormalities on urinary assessment, the AUA recommends potassium citrate and/or thiazide diuretics. The calcium oxalate management table additionally gives recommendations according to hypocitraturia, hyperoxaluria, hypercalciuria, hyperuricosuria, hypomagnesuria and hypernatriuria.
main_findings.context: AUA: standard for potassium citrate and/or thiazide diuretics. The table includes alkaline citrate or sodium bicarbonate for hypocitraturia; condition-specific measures for hyperoxaluria; thiazide or alkaline citrate for hypercalciuria; and urate-lowering or dietary measures for hyperuricosuria.

main_findings.description: Uric acid and ammonium urate stone formers are described as having a high recurrence risk. Potassium citrate raises urinary pH and sustained alkalinisation may dissolve existing uric acid stones. The AUA advises against first-line allopurinol for uric acid stone formers, whereas the EAU recommends it when urinary uric acid is high.
main_findings.context: AUA: expert opinion against first-line allopurinol; EAU: strong recommendation for allopurinol with high urinary uric acid.

main_findings.description: Cystine-stone management centres on urinary alkalinisation, dietary measures and high fluid intake. The EAU recommends tiopronin if alkalinisation and dietary treatment are ineffective.
main_findings.value: urinary pH > 7.5; AUA fluid intake at least 4 L/day; EAU fluid intake 3.5 L/day
main_findings.context: EAU: strong recommendation for tiopronin in the stated setting. The article also presents excretion-specific measures for < 3 mmol/day and > 3 mmol/day.

main_findings.description: Calcium phosphate stones may occur as brushite or carbonate apatite. The EAU recommends thiazides when hypercalciuria is present.
main_findings.context: EAU: strong recommendation. The article associates brushite with hypercalciuria and hyperphosphatemia, and carbonate apatite with infection.

main_findings.description: For struvite stones, the EAU recommends complete surgical removal and antibiotics if bacteriuria persists. The AUA offers acetohydroxamic acid only after surgical options have been exhausted.
main_findings.context: EAU: strong recommendation for removal and antibiotics in persistent bacteriuria. The review identifies acetohydroxamic acid as a urease inhibitor; the management table labels the AUA surgical-removal and acetohydroxamic-acid entry as Option.

notable_adverse_events: SWL is associated with fewer overall complications than URS and PCNL; no event rate is provided.
Routine post-URS stenting is associated with greater morbidity, and stents can cause discomfort; no rates are provided.
PCNL may be complicated by sepsis during or after the procedure, including after a sterile preoperative urine culture; no rate is provided.
Compared with standard PCNL, mini-PNL is associated with less blood loss; no rate or amount is provided.
In children, MET is associated with more side effects; no rate is provided.

In children, PCNL is associated with greater side effects; the article reports fewer tract-size-related complications, including renal extravasation and haematuria, with mini and ultra-mini PCNL; no rates are provided.
During pregnancy, temporary ureteral stents or nephrostomy require frequent exchange because of rapid encrustation; no rate is provided.
Imaging within 4 weeks after treatment may produce false-positive findings from dust particles and consequent overtreatment; no rate is provided.

subgroup_analyses: Paediatric patients: the EAU recommends US first to limit radiation exposure. It allows observation for asymptomatic lower-pole stones <7 mm when they are not struvite or cystine stones and there are no anatomical abnormalities. The AUA recommends initial conservative management, with or without MET, for ureteral stones ≤10 mm.

Paediatric patients requiring active treatment: the EAU favours SWL first for a single ureteral stone <10 mm and renal stones <20 mm, and PCNL for renal stones >20 mm. The AUA allows SWL or URS for renal stones <20 mm and SWL with stent or nephrostomy placement, or PCNL, for stones >20 mm.

Pregnancy: the EAU recommends US before MRI and reserves NCCT as the last imaging option. Both guidelines favour observation for uncomplicated, asymptomatic nephrolithiasis where possible; if it fails, URS or temporary drainage may be considered. The EAU reports better patient satisfaction, less urinary-tract irritation and less need for stent exchange with URS than with temporary stenting.

Renal transplant recipients: the EAU recommends prompt treatment of stone-related obstruction and allows SWL, URS or PCNL according to graft anatomy and function and the patient's clotting status. The review attributes reports of safe ex vivo stone surgery and URS, and effective SWL with a low risk of major complications, to cited studies.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Urological organisations publish evidence-based guidance for conditions including urolithiasis. This review compares AUA and EAU guidance on the surgical and medical management of kidney stone disease (KSD), examining the supporting evidence and recommendation grades. Both address imaging, treatment, medical therapy, paediatric patients and pregnancy. Their recommendations largely agree, although some details differ. The authors call for regular updates and for treatment decisions to reflect patient preferences, surgical expertise and individual circumstances.

document_sections.heading: 1. Introduction
document_sections.content: Urolithiasis is common worldwide, with occurrence varying by gender, climate, diet and other risks. Stone prevalence has risen yearly among people above the age of 30 across genders. Treatment and technological advances impose substantial costs: estimated global spending on KSD was USD 5.3 billion in 2014, making it the second most costly urological condition. Clinicians widely use AUA and EAU guidance for diagnosis, treatment and follow-up. The AUA publishes separate medical and surgical guidance, last updated in 2019 and 2016, respectively; the EAU's Urolithiasis guidance was last updated in 2023. The AUA assigns evidence grades A, B and C according to quality and certainty. Its surgical guidance distinguishes strong, moderate and conditional recommendations; its medical guidance uses options, recommendations and standards informed by patient risk–benefit considerations. Clinical principles and expert opinions supplement areas with insufficient evidence. The EAU uses strong and weak recommendations informed by GRADE and considers effect size, evidence certainty, outcome balance and patient preferences. Its stated aims for the 2024 update include further appraisal of endourological practice and examination of whether stone size accurately guides treatment selection. Guidelines consolidate evidence but cannot guarantee optimal outcomes, partly because updating them has limitations. Clinical expertise and individual patient circumstances must take precedence when planning care.

document_sections.heading: 2.1. Presentation and Evaluation
document_sections.content: Urolithiasis may cause fever, vomiting or loin pain, or produce no symptoms. Bladder calculi may present with recurrent UTIs, urinary frequency, terminal haematuria or suprapubic pain. Assessment should include a thorough history and examination. The EAU advises prompt investigation when the diagnosis is uncertain, pyrexia is present or the patient has a solitary kidney (strong recommendation). Choosing imaging must not postpone effective analgesia or resuscitation.

document_sections.heading: 2.2.1. Renal and Ureteric Stones
document_sections.content: For asymptomatic patients, the EAU favours initial US because it avoids radiation, costs less and can identify hydronephrosis and stones in the calyces, renal pelvis and pelvic-ureteric or vesico-ureteric junctions. For symptomatic patients, NCCT is preferred: it characterises density, diameter, volume, skin-to-stone distance and surrounding anatomy to inform treatment, and is more accurate than US or IVU (EAU: strong recommendation). Contrast-enhanced imaging is advised when collecting-system anatomy must be assessed before removal (EAU: strong recommendation). KUB X-ray can establish radiopacity but need not be obtained when NCCT is planned. The AUA recommends NCCT before PCNL (AUA: strong recommendation) and when choosing between SWL and URS (AUA: conditional recommendation); US alone is discouraged for the latter decision. Suspected substantial renal injury may warrant a DTPA or MAG-3 renogram to guide care (AUA: conditional recommendation). The EAU advises testing serum creatinine, uric acid, ionised calcium, sodium, potassium, blood cell counts and C-reactive protein, plus coagulation when intervention is intended (EAU: strong recommendation). Both organisations strongly recommend urine culture and microscopy before intervention.

document_sections.heading: 2.2.2. Bladder Stones
document_sections.content: In symptomatic patients with suspected bladder calculi, US is the initial imaging test. If symptoms persist and US is inconclusive, NCCT or cystoscopy should be considered because both are more sensitive (EAU: strong recommendation). KUB X-ray indicates radiopacity but detects stones poorly; its use for treatment planning and follow-up carries an EAU weak recommendation. Evidence is too sparse for specific paediatric bladder-stone imaging guidance. The AUA provides no bladder-stone diagnostic guidance.

document_sections.heading: 3.1. Medical Treatment
document_sections.content: Drugs discussed for MET include α-blockers, calcium channel inhibitors and PDE5 inhibitors. Meta-analyses cited by the review demonstrate a class effect for α-blockers used off-label as MET. The EAU advises considering α-blockers for distal ureteral stones >5 mm (strong recommendation); the AUA advises offering them for distal ureteral stones ≤10 mm (strong recommendation).

document_sections.heading: 3.2. Oral Chemolysis
document_sections.content: Urinary alkalinisation with alkaline citrate or sodium bicarbonate can dissolve uric acid stones, although no RCTs of this longstanding approach are available. Potassium citrate should be offered to alkalinise urine in patients with uric acid or cystine stones, but dissolution outcomes vary (AUA: expert opinion). Patients should be monitored during and after chemolysis, taught to measure urinary pH and have dosing adjusted accordingly (EAU: strong recommendation).

document_sections.heading: 3.3. Extracorporeal Shock Wave Lithotripsy (ESWL)
document_sections.content: Compared with endourological procedures such as URS and PCNL, SWL has a lower SFR but fewer overall complications. Its effectiveness depends on patient habitus, stone size, site and composition, and procedural performance. Appropriate coupling material, such as ultrasound gel, and careful fluoroscopic or US monitoring help avoid shock-wave deflection (EAU: strong recommendation). Adequate analgesia limits movement caused by pain and improves outcomes (EAU: strong recommendation). Infected stones or laboratory evidence of infection warrant antibiotics before intervention (AUA/EAU: strong recommendation). The AUA strongly advises against routine stenting for SWL; the EAU states that routine stenting does not improve SFR, although it might decrease steinstrasse. After SWL, α-blockers may facilitate fragment passage if patients are told this is off-label (AUA: moderate recommendation); the EAU likewise recommends MET after SWL. EAU-listed contraindications include uncontrolled UTIs, severe skeletal malformations, obesity, pregnancy, bleeding disorders, obstruction distal to the calculus and an arterial aneurysm near it.

document_sections.heading: 3.4. Ureteroscopy (URS)
document_sections.content: URS yields a higher SFR and better clinical outcomes than SWL; its morbidity and complications have improved with contemporary endourology. Neither organisation recommends routine pre-stenting (AUA: strong recommendation). Although the AUA notes possible SFR and operative-time advantages, it advises against pre-stenting because high-level evidence is lacking. After uncomplicated URS in patients without increased postoperative risk, stents should be avoided because they increase morbidity and are not cost-effective (EAU/AUA: strong recommendation). If a stent is inserted, α-blockers are recommended for discomfort (EAU: strong recommendation; AUA: moderate recommendation). The EAU advises removal under direct vision (strong recommendation), and the AUA favours a safety guide wire where feasible (expert opinion). The EAU suggests UAS for anticipated lengthy procedures or large or multiple renal calculi. It recommends Ho:YAG for URS across stone types (strong recommendation); TFL outcomes appear comparable, but further head-to-head clinical studies are needed. Both guidelines endorse peri-operative antibiotic prophylaxis before endoscopy. The EAU supports antegrade percutaneous URS when SWL fails and retrograde URS is unsuitable for ureteral stones; it also supports flexible URS when PCNL and SWL are unavailable, including for stones > 2 cm (EAU: strong recommendation). When removal cannot await interruption of antithrombotic treatment, URS is preferred (EAU/AUA: strong recommendation). Beyond anaesthetic risks and untreated UTIs, the EAU regards URS as safe for most patients without a specific contraindication.

document_sections.heading: 3.5. Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy (PCNL)
document_sections.content: PCNL is the initial procedure for most large renal stones because its high SFR is less constrained by stone burden or composition. Preoperative US or CT should define collecting-system and adjacent anatomy to establish a safe access route (EAU: strong recommendation); the AUA strongly advises NCCT before PCNL. The EAU considers prone and supine positioning comparably safe and advises selection according to available equipment and surgical expertise. Compared with standard PCNL (>22Fr), mini-PNL (mPNL 12-22Fr) has a similar SFR, shorter admission and less blood loss. Flexible nephroscopy should routinely help retrieve fragments beyond rigid-nephroscope reach. Normal saline irrigation should be used for PCNL and URS to avoid electrolyte disturbances (AUA: strong recommendation). After uncomplicated PCNL, tubeless treatment without nephrostomy, or totally tubeless treatment without nephrostomy or ureteral stent, should be considered for shorter admission and better postoperative pain control (EAU: strong recommendation; AUA: conditional recommendation). A change in EAU guidance is to obtain a pelvic urine or stone culture during PCNL (strong recommendation): sepsis may occur despite sterile preoperative urine, and a renal-pelvis culture can better anticipate it and identify organisms for antibiotic selection. EAU contraindications include a tumour along the access route, malignant renal tumour, pregnancy, untreated UTIs and anticoagulant therapy, which requires careful monitoring and preoperative discontinuation.

document_sections.heading: 3.6. Open Surgery and Laparoscopy
document_sections.content: Advances in endourology have made open and laparoscopic stone surgery uncommon. Both guidelines reserve these approaches for situations in which SWL, URS and PCNL are unlikely to remove the stone successfully (EAU/AUA: strong recommendation). The AUA identifies concomitant anatomical defects requiring reconstruction as one circumstance in which an open or laparoscopic operation may offer greater benefit.

document_sections.heading: 4.1. Renal Colic
document_sections.content: Acute colic from a ureteral stone usually requires emergency analgesia. Once contraindications are excluded, paracetamol and NSAIDs should be first-line options because they can relieve pain better than opioids. They also reduce inflammation and recurrent pain during conservative care (EAU: strong recommendation). Persistent pain despite analgesia calls for renal decompression and endoscopic stone removal (EAU: strong recommendation).

document_sections.heading: 4.2. Obstruction, Sepsis, Anuria
document_sections.content: Sepsis from an infected, obstructed urinary system causes substantial urolithiasis-related morbidity and mortality. Both organisations strongly advise immediate decompression by PCN or ureteric stent, with neither approach shown superior, and postponement of definitive stone treatment until sepsis resolves. Antibiotics must start without delay and may be modified after susceptibility results. Intensive-care involvement should be sought when needed. The EAU strongly advises obtaining urine during decompression.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.1. Conservative Management/Medical Expulsive Therapy (MET)
document_sections.content: Patients without stone-related complications may undergo observation with regular reassessment. The EAU refers to small stones without defining a size; spontaneous passage becomes less likely as stone size rises and varies among patients (EAU: strong recommendation). The AUA specifies ≤10 mm for observation (strong recommendation). Both organisations recommend α-blockers as MET for distal ureteric stones. In this subsection, the article describes AUA eligibility as ≤10 mm and EAU eligibility as <5 mm (AUA/EAU: strong recommendation); its earlier medical-treatment subsection instead gives the EAU threshold as >5 mm. The AUA suggests 4–6 weeks of MET before devising definitive treatment if passage fails (moderate recommendation). The EAU provides no particular interval before definitive treatment.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.2. Active Treatment
document_sections.content: SWL or URS is indicated when spontaneous passage is unlikely, stones obstruct urine flow, pain persists despite adequate analgesia, or renal function falls because of renal failure, a solitary kidney or bilateral obstruction. If the clinical presentation changes, repeat KUB X-ray, US or CT should be considered before intervention because stone position and the required management may have changed (AUA: clinical principle). Patients should be told that URS achieves a higher SFR and less often requires another procedure than SWL, whereas SWL has fewer complications and less morbidity (AUA/EAU: strong recommendation). The EAU favours URS first for proximal or distal ureteral stones >10 mm, and either URS or SWL first for stones <10 mm. Severe obesity also favours initial URS (EAU: strong recommendation). The AUA favours URS for mid- or distal-ureter stones requiring treatment, particularly those <10 mm, and offers SWL if URS is declined (strong recommendation). It excludes proximal stones from that preference because its panel did not find URS superior to SWL in SFR for proximal calculi > 10 mm. Table 1 compares EAU and AUA interventions by ureteral location and stone size.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.1. Conservative Management
document_sections.content: More asymptomatic renal calculi are being identified as imaging becomes more widely used. Observation may be offered for uncomplicated, non-obstructing calyceal stones (AUA: conditional recommendation), but their natural history and progression risk are poorly defined. Both organisations regard observation as debatable because high-quality evidence is lacking and advise active surveillance if it is chosen. The EAU recommends first follow-up at 6 months and then yearly, using US or X-ray to assess symptoms and growth; the AUA sets no interval. NCCT is recommended if intervention is being considered (EAU: strong recommendation).

document_sections.heading: 4.4.2. Active Treatment
document_sections.content: Before active treatment, stone composition should be assessed using patient history, earlier stone analyses or current CT Hounsfield Units (HU). SWL is unlikely to work for calculi with density >1000 HU (EAU: strong recommendation).

document_sections.heading: 4.4.3. Renal Pelvis or Upper/Middle Calyces Calculi
document_sections.content: For stones >20 mm, both organisations recommend PCNL first because it produces a higher SFR and fewer secondary procedures, while location, density and composition affect it less than SWL or URS (AUA/EAU: strong recommendation). If PCNL cannot be used, the EAU recommends considering flexible URS or SWL (strong recommendation). For stones <20 mm at these sites, the AUA recommends URS or SWL first because their SFR is acceptable (strong recommendation). The EAU permits SWL, URS or PCNL for 10–20 mm stones; for <10 mm, it favours SWL or URS first and PCNL second. Table 2 compares size- and location-based renal-stone interventions.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.4. Lower Pole Calculi
document_sections.content: For lower-pole stones >20 mm, the guidelines follow their recommendations for upper- and middle-pole stones. For stones ≤10 mm, the AUA favours SWL or URS first (strong recommendation); the EAU likewise places these first and PCNL second. Recommendations diverge for 10–20 mm stones. Because endoscopic treatment offers appreciable benefit over SWL, the AUA strongly advises against first-line SWL and advises explaining PCNL's higher SFR and greater morbidity (AUA: strong recommendation). The EAU recommends PCNL when SWL-unfavourable factors are present (strong recommendation); with favourable factors, SWL may be considered alongside PCNL and URS first. EAU-listed adverse factors are a narrow infundibulum, long skin-to-stone distance, long calyx, shock-wave-resistant calcium oxalate monohydrate, brushite or cystine, and a steep infundibular-pelvic angle.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.5. Bladder Stones
document_sections.content: Bladder stones descending from the upper tract may be observed, especially without symptoms. Primary stones arising without another urinary-tract abnormality and secondary stones associated with other urinary pathology are less likely to pass and generally require treatment. Transurethral, endoscopic and percutaneous approaches have comparable SFRs and shorter operations, admissions and catheterisation than open cystolithotomy. Adults should therefore be offered transurethral cystolithotripsy first, with percutaneous cystolithotripsy considered when it is not possible (EAU: strong recommendation). Open cystolithotomy may be initial treatment for very large stones (EAU: weak recommendation). If endoscopy is unsuitable, laparoscopic treatment, SWL or open cystolithotomy can be alternatives (EAU: weak recommendation), although SWL has a lower bladder-stone SFR than open or endoscopic treatment.

document_sections.heading: 5.1. Paediatric Population
document_sections.content: Children may have vague, age-dependent symptoms: older children can have haematuria, flank pain or recurrent UTIs, whereas infants may vomit, become irritable or cry. To limit radiation under ALARA, the EAU recommends initial US; inadequate findings may prompt KUB X-ray or NCCT (strong recommendation). The AUA recommends NCCT before paediatric PCNL (strong recommendation). The EAU notes little evidence for observation but allows it initially for asymptomatic lower-pole stones <7 mm without struvite or cystine composition or anatomical abnormalities. It states that MET may improve passage and pain but causes more side effects in children. The AUA recommends observation with or without MET first for ureteral stones ≤10 mm; patients or parents should be informed if MET is used off-label (AUA: moderate recommendation). Routine stenting before paediatric URS is discouraged (AUA: expert opinion). SWL, URS and PCNL generally have indications similar to those in adults. For a single ureteral stone <10 mm, the EAU favours SWL first and URS if SWL fails or cannot be used (strong recommendation). URS with lasertripsy can have good, safe outcomes when performed by surgeons experienced in paediatric complications. After failed observation or MET, the AUA recommends choosing SWL or URS according to anatomy and habitus (strong recommendation). It cautions that ultrasound-based lithotriptors may poorly visualise the ureter, particularly its middle portion, while SWL can be useful in small children for whom URS access is difficult. For renal stones <20 mm, the EAU favours SWL first (strong recommendation) and FURS may follow failed SWL, especially for lower-calyceal stones; the AUA supports SWL or URS (moderate recommendation). For renal stones >20 mm, the EAU recommends PCNL (strong recommendation). In children, PCNL's higher SFR comes with more side effects, although mini and ultra-mini PCNL have reduced complications related to tract size, including renal extravasation and haematuria. The AUA instead accepts either PCNL or SWL with stent or nephrostomy for >20 mm stones (moderate recommendation). It also favours observation with routine US surveillance for asymptomatic, non-obstructing renal stones (expert opinion). All children's stones should undergo material analysis, with subsequent metabolic assessment guided by the result (EAU: strong recommendation).

document_sections.heading: 5.2. Pregnancy
document_sections.content: Stone disease during pregnancy can be difficult to manage and warrants collaboration among radiologists, urologists, obstetricians and the patient. Although NCCT has a higher positive predictive value than MRI or US, the EAU places it last after initial US and then MRI (strong recommendation). The AUA calls for multidisciplinary discussion before diagnostic imaging (clinical principle). Uncomplicated, asymptomatic nephrolithiasis should be observed where possible (AUA/EAU: strong recommendation). If observation fails, URS or temporary decompression with a ureteral stent or nephrostomy should be considered; temporary devices need frequent replacement because they encrust rapidly (AUA: strong recommendation). The EAU reports better satisfaction, less urinary irritation and fewer stent exchanges with URS than with temporary stenting.

document_sections.heading: 5.3. Renal Transplant Patients
document_sections.content: Transplant-kidney stones are uncommon and clinically challenging. They may arise in the allograft or have been present in the donor kidney. US can detect them, with NCCT used if US is inconclusive. Obstruction needs prompt effective treatment because graft recipients depend on the transplanted solitary kidney for renal function. The EAU permits SWL, URS or PCNL according to graft anatomy and function, clotting status and other factors (weak recommendation). Treating a donor stone before transplantation may increase donor availability; a donor-kidney calculus is a relative contraindication to donation. The cited evidence describes ex vivo bench ureteroscopy or pyelolithomy immediately after donor nephrectomy as safe without impairing graft function; URS at experienced centres as safe with good donor- and recipient-kidney outcomes; and SWL for de novo graft stones as effective with low major-complication risk, although seldom used.

document_sections.heading: 5.4. Post-Procedural Imaging
document_sections.content: Fragments may remain after endourological treatment or SWL and may need additional treatment. The EAU recommends post-treatment imaging (strong recommendation), but limited high-quality evidence leaves its timing and the decision to treat fragments to clinician judgment and patient preferences. Imaging within 4 weeks may misidentify dust as residual stones and cause overtreatment. NCCT detects fragments more sensitively than X-ray, US or IVU but increases radiation exposure and may find clinically unimportant particles; its benefits and harms must be weighed. The AUA advises considering endourological treatment when residual fragments are found, particularly with infected stones (moderate recommendation).

document_sections.heading: 5.5. Recurrence Prevention and Metabolic Evaluation
document_sections.content: All newly diagnosed patients need metabolic evaluation. Initial screening includes medical, nutritional and medication histories; dipstick and microscopic urinalysis; and serum testing, including PTH when hyperparathyroidism is suspected (AUA: clinical principle). After stone passage, screening and stone analysis can distinguish high- from low-risk patients. When possible, every first stone should be analysed by X-ray diffraction or infrared spectroscopy (EAU: strong recommendation; AUA: clinical principle). Analysis should be repeated after early or late recurrence or recurrence despite medical therapy (EAU: strong recommendation). High-risk patients require metabolic assessment because medical treatment may help; first-time stone formers may also receive it for tailored nutritional guidance or, where applicable, drugs (AUA: standard). The cited evidence finds metabolism-directed dietary treatment more effective against recurrence than generic advice. Assessment should use one or two 24-h urine collections; the AUA prefers two and advises measuring at least pH, volume, calcium, uric acid, sodium, citrate, oxalate, potassium and creatinine while the patient follows a random diet (expert opinion). The EAU prefers two consecutive 24-h collections and notes that a spot sample has limited utility but can substitute when collection is impracticable, such as in children. Ideally, initial testing follows at least 20 days without stones while the patient eats normally. Both guidelines tailor diet and medication to metabolic and stone findings; the EAU also discusses general lifestyle, fluids and balanced nutrition. Both emphasise that greater fluid intake is associated with lower stone risk and recommend enough to produce a 24-h urinary volume of at least >2.5 L (EAU: strong recommendation; AUA: standard).

document_sections.heading: 5.6. Calcium Oxalate Stones
document_sections.content: The review lists hyperoxaluria, hyperuricosuria, hypocitraturia, hypomagnesuria and hypocalciuria among common metabolic abnormalities associated with calcium stones. The AUA advises potassium citrate and/or thiazide diuretics for recurrent calcium calculi even when the 24-h urine sample shows no abnormalities (standard). Table 3 presents metabolic-finding-specific EAU and AUA approaches for calcium oxalate stones, including dietary measures and medication.

document_sections.heading: 5.7. Uric Acid and Urate-Containing Stones
document_sections.content: Uric acid and ammonium urate stone formers are considered at high recurrence risk. Uric acid stones commonly accompany low urinary pH or hyperuricosuria; uncommon ammonium urate stones are associated with malnutrition, UTIs, hypokalaemia, hypophosphatemia and malabsorption. Potassium citrate can raise urinary pH, and sustained alkalinisation can dissolve existing stones. The AUA advises against first-line allopurinol for uric acid stone formers (expert opinion), whereas the EAU recommends it when urinary uric acid is high (strong recommendation). Table 4 compares recommendations for acidic urine, hyperuricosuria and ammonium urate stones.

document_sections.heading: 5.8. Cystine Stones
document_sections.content: Management centres on keeping urinary pH > 7.5 and modifying diet. Because cystine concentration influences stone formation, fluid intake is important: the AUA recommends at least 4 L/day and the EAU suggests 3.5 L/day. Sodium and protein should be restricted, and potassium citrate is used for alkalinisation (AUA: expert opinion). The EAU also supports potassium citrate and recommends tiopronin when diet and alkalinisation do not succeed (strong recommendation). Table 5 sets out approaches according to cystine excretion.

document_sections.heading: 5.9. Calcium Phosphate Stones
document_sections.content: Calcium phosphate stones can occur as brushite or carbonate apatite. Brushite is linked to hypercalciuria and hyperphosphatemia; carbonate apatite can arise with infection. Calcium phosphate stones may therefore occur with UTIs, hyperparathyroidism or renal tubular acidosis. The EAU recommends thiazides for hypercalciuria (strong recommendation). Table 6 compares measures for hypercalciuria and raised urinary pH.

document_sections.heading: 5.10. Struvite Stones
document_sections.content: Struvite stones may originate independently or result from infection of an existing stone by urease-producing bacteria. Complete surgical clearance is the first-line treatment, with antibiotics when bacteriuria persists (EAU: strong recommendation). The AUA advises that acetohydroxamic acid (AHA), a urease inhibitor, can be offered after surgical options have been exhausted (expert opinion). Table 7 also sets out EAU options for urinary acidification and persistent colonisation, and AUA advice about surveillance for reinfection and possible prophylactic antibiotics.

document_sections.heading: 6. Areas of Future Research
document_sections.content: Future studies should report costs and patient-reported outcomes. Regular guidance updates should address emerging lasers, day-case surgery, smaller scopes, artificial intelligence and suction devices. Consistent definitions and reporting would make outcomes easier to compare and support counselling and decisions.

document_sections.heading: 7. Conclusions
document_sections.content: KSD is prevalent worldwide and is increasing across ages, races and sexes, with diet and climate among the contributing factors. Continuing endourological innovation is expected to change future care. AUA and EAU guidelines cover many aspects of management through evidence-based guidance; although some size-dependent recommendations differ, most management principles agree. The authors ask future studies to include patient-reported outcomes and measurable, comparable endpoints reported more consistently. They recommend regular guideline updates while stressing that care must remain individualised to patient preferences, surgical expertise and other personal factors.

drugs_and_therapies.context: Appears in recommendations for stone prevention associated with hypercalciuria.

drugs_and_therapies.name: Pyridoxine
drugs_and_therapies.context: Listed for primary hyperoxaluria type 1.

drugs_and_therapies.name: Allopurinol
drugs_and_therapies.context: Discussed for hyperuricosuria; the AUA advises against its first-line use for uric acid stone formers.

drugs_and_therapies.name: Febuxostat
drugs_and_therapies.context: Listed as a second-line option for hyperuricosuria.

drugs_and_therapies.name: Magnesium
drugs_and_therapies.context: Listed in the calcium oxalate stone management table.

drugs_and_therapies.name: L-methionine
drugs_and_therapies.context: Listed for urinary pH findings in the uric acid and calcium phosphate stone tables.

drugs_and_therapies.name: tiopronin
drugs_and_therapies.context: Discussed for cystine stones when dietary measures and alkalinisation are ineffective.

drugs_and_therapies.name: ammonium chloride
drugs_and_therapies.context: Listed among EAU measures for struvite stones.

drugs_and_therapies.name: Methionine
drugs_and_therapies.context: Listed as an alternative urinary acidification measure for struvite stones.

drugs_and_therapies.name: acetohydroxamic acid (AHA)
drugs_and_therapies.context: The AUA discusses offering it for struvite stones after surgical options are exhausted.

biomarkers_and_genes.name: urinary pH
biomarkers_and_genes.context: Guides urinary alkalinisation or acidification and features in stone-specific recommendations.

biomarkers_and_genes.name: Hounsfield Units (HU)
biomarkers_and_genes.context: CT-derived stone density helps assess composition and the likely effectiveness of SWL.

biomarkers_and_genes.name: stone size
biomarkers_and_genes.context: Used with stone location to distinguish observation and procedural options.

biomarkers_and_genes.name: stone composition
biomarkers_and_genes.context: Considered before active treatment and in recurrence prevention.

biomarkers_and_genes.name: stone analysis
biomarkers_and_genes.context: Used to classify recurrence risk and guide metabolic evaluation.

biomarkers_and_genes.name: serum creatinine
biomarkers_and_genes.context: Included among EAU-recommended blood tests when intervention is planned.

biomarkers_and_genes.name: uric acid
biomarkers_and_genes.context: Measured in serum before intervention and in urinary metabolic assessment.

biomarkers_and_genes.name: ionised calcium
biomarkers_and_genes.context: Included among EAU-recommended serum tests.

biomarkers_and_genes.name: sodium
biomarkers_and_genes.context: Included in serum testing and urinary metabolic assessment.

biomarkers_and_genes.name: potassium
biomarkers_and_genes.context: Included in serum testing and urinary metabolic assessment.

biomarkers_and_genes.name: blood cell counts
biomarkers_and_genes.context: Included among EAU-recommended tests.

biomarkers_and_genes.name: C-reactive protein
biomarkers_and_genes.context: Included among EAU-recommended tests.

biomarkers_and_genes.name: parathyroid hormone levels (PTH)
biomarkers_and_genes.context: Included in initial screening when hyperparathyroidism is suspected.

biomarkers_and_genes.name: calcium
biomarkers_and_genes.context: Measured in 24-h urine samples.

biomarkers_and_genes.name: citrate
biomarkers_and_genes.context: Measured in 24-h urine samples.

biomarkers_and_genes.name: oxalate
biomarkers_and_genes.context: Measured in 24-h urine samples.

biomarkers_and_genes.name: creatinine
biomarkers_and_genes.context: Measured in 24-h urine samples.

biomarkers_and_genes.name: volume
biomarkers_and_genes.context: Assessed in 24-h urine samples and used to guide fluid-intake advice.

biomarkers_and_genes.name: cystine excretion
biomarkers_and_genes.context: Used to organise cystine stone recommendations in the management table.

biomarkers_and_genes.name: urine culture
biomarkers_and_genes.context: Recommended before intervention; sampling during decompression or PCNL is also discussed.

biomarkers_and_genes.name: stone culture
biomarkers_and_genes.context: Collection during PCNL is discussed to help identify organisms and guide antibiotics.

scales_and_classifications.name: AUA
scales_and_classifications.description: The guideline system compared with EAU; its evidence grades are A, B, and C, with recommendation terminology differing between its medical and surgical guidelines.

scales_and_classifications.name: EAU
scales_and_classifications.description: The guideline system compared with AUA; it classifies recommendations as “strong” or “weak”.

scales_and_classifications.name: GRADE
scales_and_classifications.description: A methodology whose guiding concept informs the EAU classification of recommendations.

scales_and_classifications.name: ALARA (As Low As Reasonably Achievable)
scales_and_classifications.description: A radiation-exposure principle considered when imaging children.

scales_and_classifications.name: high or low risk for stone formation
scales_and_classifications.description: A classification based on initial screening and stone analysis after stone passage.

scales_and_classifications.name: primary
scales_and_classifications.description: A bladder stone category described as forming without another urinary tract abnormality.

scales_and_classifications.name: secondary
scales_and_classifications.description: A bladder stone category occurring with another urinary tract pathology.

scales_and_classifications.name: Migratory bladder stones
scales_and_classifications.description: Bladder stones that have passed from the upper urinary tract.
